VCU enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a 27-7 overall record and a 15-3 Atlantic 10 record, then added the A-10 tournament title with a 70-62 win over Dayton on March 15, 2026. The Atlantic 10’s official statistics page lists VCU at 27-7 overall, while VCU’s official recap of the March 6 regular-season finale at Dayton confirmed the Rams finished the regular season 24-7 and 15-3 in league play. ([admin.atlantic10.com](https://admin.atlantic10.com/stats.aspx?path=mbball&year=2025))

Offensively, VCU’s profile is concrete: through 34 games the Rams averaged 81.6 points per game, ranking second in the A-10, and posted a +10.1 scoring margin. Before the final stretch they were at 83.7 points per game through 27 contests, shooting 46.7 percent from the field, 36.5 percent from three, and averaging 14.6 assists against 11.0 turnovers. In league play they averaged 80.6 points, shot 46.4 percent overall, and made 8.3 threes per game. ([admin.atlantic10.com](https://admin.atlantic10.com/stats.aspx?path=mbball&year=2025))

The tape and game recaps show a modern spread attack built around paint touches from Lazar Djokovic, dribble-drive creation from Terrence Hill Jr. and Brandon Jennings, and kick-out shooting from wings like Jadrian Tracey and Tyrell Ward. Specific examples: against Dayton on February 6, VCU scored 99 points, built a 50-27 halftime lead, and posted a 30-6 fast-break edge, evidence that the Rams aggressively turn stops into early offense. In that game, Tracey scored a career-high 26 on 9-of-12 shooting and 6-of-9 from three, while VCU got 38 free-throw attempts, showing both transition pressure and downhill rim attacks. Against Saint Joseph’s on January 19, VCU generated 17 assists on 27 made baskets, won the second-half glass 20-12, grabbed eight offensive rebounds after halftime, and turned those into 13 second-chance points; that is a specific indicator that their half-court offense is not just first-action dependent, but also built on weak-side crashing and put-back pressure. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/news/2026/2/7/mens-basketball-vcu-routs-dayton-behind-traceys-26.aspx))

Their half-court tendencies also show up late in games. In the March 3 win over George Mason, when the Patriots cut the margin to 57-54 with seven minutes left, VCU answered with a Michael Belle layup, a Djokovic right-wing three, then later a Hill three with 3:58 left and a Hill driving layup with nine seconds left. That sequence is revealing: VCU trusts interior touch, inside-out threes, and ball-screen shot creation from Hill in leverage possessions. Against Richmond on January 27, with the Spiders trimming the lead to four with 1:06 remaining, Hill answered with a pull-up jumper and VCU got the defensive stop to finish the game. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/news/2026/3/3/mens-basketball-hill-djokovic-provide-clutch-buckets-as-rams-hold-off-patriots-70-65.aspx))

Defensively, VCU is not the old “Havoc” version in pure volume terms, but the philosophy still leans toward disruption, pressure at the point of attack, and rim protection behind it. Through 27 games the Rams had forced more turnovers than they committed, averaging 7.5 steals and 4.7 blocks per game; in league play opponents shot 45.7 percent overall and 33.2 percent from three. The frontcourt anchor is Djokovic, who had 34 blocks through 26 games and later produced a career-high four blocks against Dayton on February 6. Brandon Jennings had 41 steals through 27 games, giving them a pressure guard who can bother handlers and jump passing lanes. ([static.vcuathletics.com](https://static.vcuathletics.com/custompages/sports/mbkb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

Specific defensive tendencies appear in game results. VCU held Richmond, one of the better three-point teams in the league, to 5-of-15 from deep on January 27. They held Dayton to 37 percent shooting in the 99-73 blowout on February 6. In the March 3 win over George Mason, they closed the game by forcing the Patriots into a half-court finish after Hill’s late layup gave VCU a 70-65 edge with nine seconds left. But their defensive flaws are also documented: Saint Louis beat them 71-62 on January 7 while VCU shot only 29 percent, and the Billikens outscored them 40-24 in the paint; George Mason beat them 86-80 on January 10 by shooting 56 percent overall and 60 percent in the second half, plus winning the paint 44-36. Those losses show that physical frontcourts and efficient paint scoring can compromise VCU’s pressure scheme if the first line does not contain the ball. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/news/2026/1/28/mens-basketball-rams-pounce-early-hold-off-spiders-late-rally-in-rivalry-win.aspx))

Coaching philosophy requires a date clarification. The 2025-26 VCU team was coached by Phil Martelli Jr., not Ryan Odom. VCU’s own January 19 recap explicitly identifies “VCU head coach Phil Martelli Jr.” Martelli’s documented in-game adjustment history is visible in the results above: versus Saint Joseph’s on January 19, his team answered a tight game by dominating the second-half boards 20-12 and producing 13 second-chance points; versus Richmond on January 27, VCU protected a lead by shifting to free-throw pressure and late-clock shotmaking, going 19-of-24 at the line in the second half; versus George Mason on March 3, the Rams answered a 15-7 early deficit and a later 57-54 squeeze by using Belle’s interior score and late Hill/Djokovic shot creation. Those are specific examples of adjustment toward rebounding emphasis, foul-pressure offense, and matchup scoring late. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/news/2026/1/19/mens-basketball-belle-jennings-fuel-vcu-second-half-rally.aspx))

Clutch and late-game execution is a real strength. On March 3, 2026, VCU beat George Mason 70-65 in a game with three ties and seven lead changes; Hill hit a three with 3:58 left and a layup with nine seconds left, while Djokovic hit a go-ahead stretch three during a 8-0 stabilizing burst. On March 6, 2026, VCU won at Dayton 68-62 in a game with seven ties and 12 lead changes, and the largest lead by either side was only six points. On January 27, 2026, VCU beat Richmond 77-69 after the Spiders cut it to four with 1:06 left; Hill’s pull-up jumper sealed it. The flip side came January 10, when George Mason answered VCU’s 56-55 lead with 9:23 left by ripping off an 8-0 run and handing the Rams an 86-80 loss. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/news/2026/3/3/mens-basketball-hill-djokovic-provide-clutch-buckets-as-rams-hold-off-patriots-70-65.aspx))

Key players start with Terrence Hill Jr., the team’s leading scorer at 14.6 points per game through 27 games, with 2.9 assists and 38.0 percent three-point shooting. His late-game scoring is documented by 16 points against George Mason on March 3, 13 points and a career-high eight assists against Saint Joseph’s on January 19, and 14 points against Dayton on February 6. Lazar Djokovic is the interior fulcrum: 13.7 points, 5.7 rebounds, 34 blocks through 26 games, then 23 points on 7-of-9 shooting and 9-of-9 free throws at George Mason on January 10, 16 points and six rebounds at Dayton on March 6, and 13 points, seven boards, four blocks versus Dayton on February 6. Jadrian Tracey gave them perimeter volatility and shotmaking, including a career-high 26 against Dayton on February 6 and 14 points on Senior Night against George Mason on March 3. Brandon Jennings supplied two-way guard play with 8.8 points and 41 steals through 27 games, plus 18 points and 4-of-4 from three against Saint Joseph’s. Michael Belle was the glue big/wing off the bench, scoring a career-high 20 against Saint Joseph’s on 9-of-11 shooting and adding five rebounds, three steals, and two blocks. ([static.vcuathletics.com](https://static.vcuathletics.com/custompages/sports/mbkb/2025-26/teamcume.htm))

Notable wins: the 99-73 destruction of Dayton on February 6 revealed VCU’s ceiling when its pace and transition game get rolling; the 30-6 fast-break margin is one of the clearest style markers on the résumé. The 70-65 win over George Mason on March 3 showed poise against a physical top-tier A-10 opponent and confirmed Hill/Djokovic as the closing duo. The 68-62 road win at Dayton on March 6 showed they can survive a grinder away from home. Earlier, the 86-68 neutral-floor win over Virginia Tech on November 28 was a useful nonconference data point showing VCU’s athletic edge can overwhelm major-conference teams in open-floor settings. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/news/2026/2/7/mens-basketball-vcu-routs-dayton-behind-traceys-26.aspx))

Notable losses: the 71-62 home loss to Saint Louis on January 7 revealed a vulnerability when the offense bogs down; VCU shot a season-low 29 percent and got outscored 40-24 in the paint. The 86-80 loss at George Mason on January 10 showed their defense can be bent by efficient interior offense and foul pressure, as Mason shot 56 percent and went 21-of-24 at the line. The 81-78 home loss to New Mexico on December 10 and 80-77 neutral loss to Utah State on November 7 both underscored that VCU has had problems finishing against quality opponents when games become possession-for-possession late. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/news/2026/1/7/mens-basketball-cold-shooting-dooms-rams-against-billikens.aspx))

For the head coach’s NCAA tournament history, again the date clarification matters: Phil Martelli Jr. is VCU’s 2025-26 head coach, and he does not have a prior NCAA tournament history as a Division I head coach documented in the sources reviewed. Ryan Odom, the previous VCU coach, is no longer the VCU coach for this tournament cycle. Sports-Reference lists Odom with three NCAA tournament appearances and a 1-3 record as a head coach: 2018 at UMBC, where he reached the Round of 32 by beating Virginia before losing to Kansas State; 2023 at Utah State, which lost in the First Round; and 2025 at VCU, which lost in the First Round. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/news/2026/1/19/mens-basketball-belle-jennings-fuel-vcu-second-half-rally.aspx))

Bottom line: this VCU team is an 81.6-point-per-game, pressure-to-transition club with a dependable late-game creator in Hill, an efficient interior scorer and rim protector in Djokovic, and enough shooting from Tracey, Jennings, Ward, and Belle to punish help. The path to beating them is to win the paint, stay organized against their transition game, and force them into a lower-possession half-court contest like Saint Louis and George Mason did in their January wins. ([admin.atlantic10.com](https://admin.atlantic10.com/stats.aspx?path=mbball&year=2025))

VCU enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with the profile of a dangerous mid-major that is much more solidly built than the usual “upset trendy” stereotype. Broadly across public efficiency systems, the Rams grade as a top-50 national team and a clear tournament-caliber club. In Bart Torvik’s T-Rank data for 2026, VCU sits No. 48 nationally at 27-7 with an adjusted offensive efficiency of 119.2 and an adjusted defensive efficiency of 103.1, good for a strong but not elite overall efficiency margin. That same Torvik snapshot shows VCU with a 68.7 adjusted tempo, placing them on the faster side of the national median without being truly extreme. A publicly indexed KenPom-style ranking page lists VCU No. 46 nationally, with the offense ranked 49th and the defense 64th, which is directionally consistent with the Torvik read: good on both ends, a little better offensively than many casual observers would assume. RotoWire’s 2026 team page also places VCU at NET No. 43 and shows a 27-7 overall record with a 15-3 league mark. 

The key statistical takeaway is that this is not vintage “Havoc-only” VCU. The offense is the clearer strength. RotoWire lists VCU’s raw offensive efficiency at 1.19 points per possession and defensive efficiency at 1.03, with offensive eFG% at 54.08% and defensive eFG% allowed at 48.85%. Using VCU’s official cumulative team totals, the Rams have made 909 field goals and 317 threes on 1,974 attempts, which works out to an exact effective field-goal percentage of 54.08%. They have also attempted 863 free throws against 1,974 field-goal attempts, an exact free-throw rate of 43.72, which is a major offensive driver and an unusually strong number for a team that also shoots 36.7% from three. Official team totals show VCU averaging 81.6 points per game while allowing 71.5, shooting 46.0% from the field, 36.7% from three, and 73.9% from the line. 

At the possession level, the offensive shape is clear. VCU’s approximate offensive turnover rate is 13.20%, matching RotoWire’s listed figure and indicating a very clean offense. The Rams also have a 43.77% three-point attempt rate, meaning nearly 44% of their shots come from beyond the arc. That matters because it sharpens the identity: VCU spaces the floor, values the ball, and gets to the line. On Torvik, their offensive efficiency components are similarly strong: 54.1 eFG%, 15.2 TO%, 32.3 OR%, 43.7 FT rate, and 43.8 3-point rate. Those numbers collectively describe a modern, analytically sound offense rather than a chaos-first grinder. 

Defensively, the picture is good but less overwhelming than brand perception suggests. Torvik gives VCU a 48.9 defensive eFG% allowed, 17.2 turnover rate forced, 29.9 defensive rebounding figure in the displayed split, 33.1 free-throw rate allowed, and 34.7 opponent three-point attempt rate. RotoWire’s defensive side has them allowing a 48.85 eFG%, forcing turnovers at only 15.03%, and allowing a 33.08 opponent FTA/FGA. The most important divergence from conventional wisdom is right there: this VCU team is not an elite turnover-forcing defense by national standards. The defense is competent, active, and generally efficient, but the havoc component is toned down. If an opponent handles ball pressure, the Rams are less likely than classic VCU teams to completely detonate a game with live-ball takeaways. 

The resume context also matters. RotoWire lists VCU at 2-4 in Quad 1, 5-3 in Quad 2, 9-0 in Quad 3, and 9-0 in Quad 4; the NET résumé page shows essentially the same shape, with VCU at 2-4 in Quad 1, 5-3 in Quad 2, 9-0 in Quad 3, and 11-0 in Quad 4 through its March 10 update. That is the résumé of a team that handled its business consistently and supplemented that with enough high-end wins to be safely in the field, but not enough elite wins to be seeded aggressively. Strength-of-schedule data is harder to pin down exactly from public sources, but the available evidence points to roughly average-to-slightly-above-average schedule difficulty nationally rather than anything punitive. DRatings listed VCU’s SOS at No. 107 at one point in season, and Loyola Chicago’s March 6 game notes described VCU as having a top-75 non-conference strength of schedule. The synthesis is straightforward: VCU challenged itself enough to validate the numbers, but this is still an Atlantic 10 résumé, not a power-conference gauntlet. 

Recent form is one of the strongest parts of the profile. Betting analysis published March 6 described VCU as 23-7 and 9-1 over its previous 10 games. Loyola Chicago’s March 6 notes had VCU at 23-7 overall and also 9-1 in its last 10 at that point. Since then, public team pages and tournament references show VCU improving to 27-7 and winning the Atlantic 10 tournament, indicating that the Rams carried strong late-season form into March. That trend aligns with a first-year team under Phil Martelli Jr. finding coherence over time: the offensive floor stayed high because they protected the ball and generated efficient shots, while the defense held up well enough for the overall efficiency margin to stabilize in top-50 territory. 

From a forecasting perspective, the most interesting divergence from the eye test is that VCU’s reputation likely undersells the offense and oversells the defense. The brand says relentless pressure, ugly games, and defense-first basketball. The actual 2025-26 statistical profile says something closer to this: a balanced, tournament-worthy team with a top-50 offense, a good-not-great defense, strong free-throw generation, real perimeter volume, and unusually low offensive mistakes. That makes VCU less random than some upset-minded mid-majors. They are not just trying to drag opponents into a bar fight; they can score efficiently in a game played at a normal pace. 

The practical implication for the NCAA Tournament is that VCU is credible against high-major opponents because their offense travels. Low turnover rate, strong eFG%, high free-throw rate, and substantial three-point volume are exactly the traits that keep underdogs live. The caution flag is that they do not appear to have a truly elite defensive carrying tool. If they run into a disciplined, physically stronger offense that wins the glass and avoids fouling, VCU’s margin for error narrows. But as a statistical matter, this is a real team, not a résumé illusion: approximately top-45 NET, top-50 in Torvik and KenPom-adjacent ranking, adjusted efficiency around 119 per 100 on offense and 103 on defense, pace around 69 possessions per 40, and an offensive profile built on shot quality, spacing, and foul pressure. That is the profile of a legitimately dangerous 2026 tournament team.

VCU enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a pressure-driven, tempo-sensitive team that wins with depth, rim pressure, and defensive event creation more than with pure half-court shotmaking. Through 34 games, the Rams averaged 81.6 points, allowed 71.5, forced 11.9 opponent turnovers per game (406 in 34 games), and posted a +9.5 scoring margin while shooting 46.0% from the field and 36.7% from three. Their own ball security is strong at 10.5 turnovers per game, so the profile is not “reckless pressure team”; it is a team that wants to speed you up defensively without playing sloppy offensively. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/sports/mbball/stats))

Stylistically, VCU is most dangerous when games become physical and possession-fragmented. They get to the foul line often: 863 free-throw attempts in 34 games, or 25.4 attempts per game, which is a major part of how they maintain offensive efficiency even on nights when the jump shot is only average. Specific examples: in a 99-73 win over Dayton on February 6, VCU scored 31 points at the line; in a 89-75 win over Loyola Chicago on January 30, they took 29 free throws; and in a 77-69 win over Richmond on January 27, they went 22-for-27 at the stripe. The specific tactic that disrupts this is to wall off the lane with length and avoid bailout fouls. When opponents kept VCU to lower-efficiency shotmaking without sending them repeatedly to the line, the Rams were far more beatable: they shot 18-of-63 against Saint Louis in a 71-62 home loss on January 7, 20-of-56 in a 89-74 loss at Vanderbilt on November 27, and 21-of-64 in a 88-75 loss at Saint Louis on February 20. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/sports/mbball/stats))

Against pressure and zone looks, the evidence says VCU is not fragile, but it can be dragged into lower-quality half-court possessions if the first action is disrupted. Their season turnover rate is low overall, yet in the more uncomfortable games the turnover number rose: 19 turnovers vs. Utah State on November 7, 17 vs. Saint Peter’s on November 12, 15 at Fordham on February 3, and 16 at Saint Louis on February 20. Those are named examples of opponents getting VCU off rhythm. Fordham held VCU to only 63 points despite losing, and Saint Louis beat VCU twice while holding them to 62 and 75; in the January 7 game VCU shot only 28.6% from the field and 25.0% from three. That is the clearest evidence that crowding the paint, shrinking driving gaps, and forcing VCU to win with late-clock jumpers can work. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/sports/mbball/stats))

Preferred pace: VCU wants the game in the low- to mid-70 possession environment, or at minimum in an up-and-down rhythm where their depth and pressure accumulate. Their scoring profile supports that: 103 vs. Wagner, 101 vs. Coppin State, 105 vs. American, 100 vs. Rider, 93 at Duquesne, 99 vs. Dayton, 89 vs. Loyola Chicago, 89 vs. George Washington. When opponents forced a slower, more half-court game, VCU’s output fell sharply: 63 at Fordham, 62 vs. Saint Louis, 68 at Dayton, 70 vs. George Mason, 71 vs. Duquesne, 75 at Davidson. To beat them, you do not just “play slow”; you must make them execute repeatedly in the half court and limit live-ball turnovers that ignite their runs. George Mason nearly did that in a 70-65 loss on March 3, and Dayton did it twice in March-level games, losing 68-62 on March 6 and 70-62 in the A-10 title game. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/sports/mbball/stats))

Size and athleticism by position matter. In the backcourt, Nyk Lewis is a smaller creator-type guard, while Terrence Hill Jr. gives them scoring punch and downhill burst; Hill led VCU in multiple late-season wins, including 20 at Richmond on February 14, 20 vs. Duquesne on March 13, 18 vs. Saint Joseph’s on March 14, and 16 vs. George Mason on March 3. That means opponents need a sturdy point-of-attack defender on Lewis and a bigger wing stopper for Hill. On the wing/forward line, Lazar Djokovic is the key size mismatch piece; he led VCU with 26 at La Salle on February 11, 20 at Davidson on January 24, 19 at Saint Louis on February 20, and 16 at Dayton on March 6. Barry Evans and Jadrian Tracey stretch the floor around him, while Brandon Jennings adds rebounding from the guard line, posting seven rebounds at Dayton on March 6. The frontcourt is more about mobility and collective rebounding than overwhelming one-on-one post dominance, so a truly big, physical 5 can move them off spots more than an undersized switch-big can. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2670/season/2026))

Offensively, VCU is more team-offense than isolation offense. Their 479 assists on 909 made field goals means 52.7% of their baskets were assisted, which strongly suggests they are not primarily an isolation team. Their season assist-to-turnover ratio was 1.34, another indicator of a connected offense. However, in tighter games that number dropped: only five assists in the 70-65 win over George Mason on March 3, seven assists in the 62-71 loss to Saint Louis on January 7, and eight assists in the 75-69 win at Davidson on January 24. That is the exact profile shift to target: blow up first action, top-lock shooters, sit on middle drives, and force VCU’s guards to generate late-clock one-on-one offense. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/sports/mbball/stats))

On transition tendencies, VCU’s raw scoring and steal volume show a team that wants to manufacture offense before the defense is set. They averaged 7.4 steals per game and scored 81.6 per game, numbers consistent with a transition-friendly model. Defensively, their transition defense is best when their own offense is under control; when they turned it over more or were forced into poor shots, they became easier to run on. The losses illustrate it: Vanderbilt scored 89 on 52.9% shooting and 50.0% from three; George Mason scored 86 on 47.6% shooting in the January 10 win over VCU; New Mexico scored 81 on 50.0% shooting and 44.4% from three on December 10. Those named games are your evidence that if you survive the initial pressure and get into early offense, VCU can be scored on before its help structure is loaded. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/sports/mbball/stats))

Coaching adaptability under Ryan Odom looks solid on a game-to-game basis and credible within games, though not wildly schematic. The best concrete evidence is result-based: after losing to Dayton 71-62 on January 7, VCU beat Dayton 99-73 on February 6, then 68-62 on March 6, then 70-62 in the A-10 final on March 15. That is a four-game sample against the same opponent with a clear adjustment arc in VCU’s favor. VCU’s official recap of the March 6 game noted the Rams shot 52% in the second half while holding Dayton to 34% after the break, evidence of effective halftime adjustment on both ends. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2670/season/2026))

Concrete gameplan: To beat this team you must 1) protect the ball well enough to avoid feeding its pressure game; VCU is far less explosive when opponents keep turnovers down, 2) build a disciplined paint wall and make Djokovic, Evans, and Tracey beat you with contested jumpers instead of free throws, 3) force a half-court game by cutting off run-outs after misses and using longer offensive possessions, 4) attack their smaller guards with size, especially through post mismatches and deep seals from bigger wings, and 5) punish them in the first 8 seconds of your offense after you break pressure, because Vanderbilt, George Mason, New Mexico, and Saint Louis all showed VCU can be scored on when the defense is not fully set. If you let VCU live at the line, create steals, and rotate fresh scorers like Hill and Djokovic into advantage spots, they can bury you fast. But if you make them play a clean, slower, low-foul game, the evidence from Saint Louis, Fordham, Dayton, and George Mason says they become much more ordinary. ([vcuathletics.com](https://vcuathletics.com/sports/mbball/stats))
